content: The mixed-methods study revealed that 53% of participants were more concerned about the transmission of Ebola or Marburg viruses than the adverse effects associated with the use of personal protective equipment (PPE). Meanwhile, 47% expressed equal concern for both virus transmission and PPE-related adverse effects. Healthcare workers emphasized that reducing the risk of virus transmission is a critical outcome, achievable only through the proper implementation of infection prevention and control (IPC) measures. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) members concluded that there was likely no significant variability or uncertainty in how much people value the primary outcomes. They did not expect substantial variability in values and preferences regarding infection prevention and control guidelines for Ebola and Marburg diseases. In the mixed-methods study, most participants indicated that Option C (washing/disinfecting the outer glove, removing it, washing/disinfecting the inner glove, and putting on a new outer glove between patients) requires more resources. The GDG judged that Option A (washing/disinfecting the outer glove between patients) would result in moderate cost savings compared to Option C, while Option B (washing/disinfecting the outer glove, removing it, and putting on a new outer glove between patients) would result in negligible cost differences compared to Option C. Although no studies on cost-effectiveness were available, the GDG believed that Option C likely offers better cost-effectiveness compared to Options A and B. Qualitative data from the study suggested that Options A and B have fewer equity concerns than Option C. In some lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), healthcare workers may face limited access to hand hygiene facilities, including consistent water supplies, and the availability and quality of gloves may contribute to inequities. Additionally, individuals with sensitivities to alcohol-based hand rubs (ABHR) or chlorine solutions may be disadvantaged when using Option C. The GDG determined that health equity would likely be reduced with Option A compared to Option C, while Option B would probably have no impact on health equity. The GDG noted that Options A and B are inconsistent with the World Health Organization’s (WHO) My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene framework. Option A was deemed unsuitable when considering the risk of transmission of other pathogens, such as HIV. The mixed-methods study showed that 17% of participants found Option C acceptable, while 44% indicated that removing both pairs of gloves, cleaning hands, and putting on new gloves was acceptable. Those favoring this approach highlighted its potential to reduce cross-contamination among patients, provided the inner glove remains uncontaminated. However, concerns were raised about the time required to perform this process, especially in high-workload settings. While 19% of participants found Option A acceptable, the GDG determined it was not ideal and decided not to consider it further, as it did not align with WHO’s hand hygiene framework. Another 19% of participants found Option B acceptable. Healthcare workers in the study preferred removing outer gloves to protect patients and washing inner gloves to protect themselves from potential contamination due to compromised glove integrity. However, they expressed concerns about the feasibility of this option, as placing a new outer glove over a wet inner glove can be challenging and time-consuming in high-workload areas. During discussions, the GDG noted that not specifying a method of disinfection might affect the recommendations. For Option C, the GDG highlighted the risk of tearing the outer gloves during removal and potential damage to the inner gloves during the disinfection process. They also noted that this option is more time-consuming, potentially reducing the time available for patient care. Some participants suggested that washing outer gloves alone might be acceptable for low-soiling events, but concerns were raised about possible tears in the inner gloves and skin exposure when changing both gloves in an Ebola treatment center (ETC) setting. The GDG emphasized that patients are key stakeholders to consider, as the different options have varying impacts on transmission risks. Acceptability to patients may differ from acceptability to healthcare workers. The GDG retained Option C as an intervention to consider, as it aligns with the current WHO recommendation and would be used as the intervention arm during evaluations. The objectives of hand hygiene and glove disinfection between patients are twofold: to protect healthcare workers and to protect patients. The GDG extensively discussed the findings from the mixed-methods study and weighed these results, along with their own experiences, in decision-making. They acknowledged that while Option C may be challenging to implement, it is acceptable to healthcare workers. A conditional recommendation was made to uphold the existing 2014 guidance: wash/disinfect the outer gloves, remove the outer gloves, wash/disinfect the inner gloves, and put on a new pair of outer gloves between patients. Regarding hand hygiene products, 45% of participants found ABHR acceptable, 34% found chlorine acceptable, and 21% found soap and water acceptable. Participants noted that ABHR is highly effective, less corrosive than chlorine, gentler on the skin, and quick to use. Some suggested that soap and water should be the first choice if hands or gloves are visibly soiled, although this method requires time for drying and may result in splashing. Chlorine was noted for its effectiveness in killing the virus, but concerns were raised about its potential adverse effects. The GDG judged that Options A and B are probably acceptable. About half of the study participants found Option A to be the most feasible, as it is less wasteful if the inner glove remains intact. However, it is more time-consuming, particularly in high-workload areas. Participants also noted that this option is most feasible in settings with limited glove availability. Those who rated Option B as the most feasible highlighted that the outer glove often needs replacement due to soiling. In terms of feasibility for glove disinfection or hand hygiene products, 38% of participants found ABHR feasible, 37% found chlorine solutions feasible, and 25% found soap and water feasible. Supporters of soap and water cited its availability and low cost but raised concerns about contaminating the water supply. Proponents of ABHR emphasized its ease of use, quick drying, portability, and local production potential, as well as its independence from running water. Advocates for chlorine stressed its effectiveness in killing the virus but noted its potential adverse effects. The GDG noted that in large treatment centers with high patient volumes, Options A or B would be more feasible than Option C. Overall, the GDG judged that Option A is feasible and Option B is probably feasible. Given that Option C is the current WHO recommendation, the GDG decided to retain it as an option for consideration and evaluation. The GDG extensively discussed the lack of evidence-based risk assessment algorithms for classifying healthcare worker exposure risks. They noted that the West African Ebola epidemic was the first outbreak during which researchers attempted to develop such an algorithm. Disparities in infection rates between expatriate and local healthcare workers may be attributed to inadequate PPE, insufficient IPC practices, or community transmission among local workers. Studies on expatriate healthcare workers in Ebola treatment units reported high exposure rates but no confirmed infections, complicating efforts to create evidence-based algorithms. Practical implementation considerations include conducting exposure assessments for healthcare workers with occupational exposure to suspected or confirmed Ebola or Marburg patients. Standard operating procedures (SOPs) should be available for managing exposures, including immediate washing of affected skin, safe removal of PPE, and reporting the exposure to supervisors. All healthcare workers should undergo exposure assessments conducted by occupational health or IPC focal points to evaluate the level of exposure risk and subsequent management.
